newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin fights pneumonia, Lebed sees early poll.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin fights pneumonia, Lebed sees early poll.

text.p: The condition of President Boris Yeltsin, who is fighting pneumonia, has stabilised and he began working from his Moscow hospital room, but in the wings at least one leading political foe is gearing up for an early election.
A statement issued by the Kremlin after doctors examined the 65-year-old leader early on Sunday said his blood pressure, pulse and temperature were all normal.
"To a significant degree, his activity has increased, and B.N. Yeltsin has begun to work on documents," the bulletin said.
But outspoken retired paratroop general Alexander Lebed, 46, seen by some political analysts as Russia's next leader, said on Sunday he foresaw an early election that he would win.
"I want to be president and I will be president," Lebed said in an interview with Russia's Channel Six television.
Asked if he was sure an early election would be called because of the president's health and whether he was ready to take part and win, he replied: "Yes".
He said there was no chance of the poll taking place as late as 2000, the year when it must be held.

Even commercial NTV television, loyal to the Kremlin, issued a grim warning to the president. "For society, the president's illness is mostly not a medical problem, but a political one," it commented in its Itogi analytical programme.
"While the medical forecast is optimistic enough, the political one is mostly unfavourable," it added.

Yeltsin checked into Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital on Wednesday with pneumonia in both lungs, just two months after undergoing quintuple heart bypass surgery and only two weeks after returning to work in the Kremlin.
Pneumonia causes a serious infection or inflammation in one or both lungs, and if both lungs are affected it is considered more serious and harder to treat.

On Sunday the Kremlin did not say when Yeltsin would leave hospital, but chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said on Friday he expected the president to spend another three days there and then three weeks recovering. Mironov also said Yeltsin was depressed by his latest bout of illness.

The president's continued absence from the Kremlin has raised concern that the man who once symbolised the vigour of the new democratic Russia will not have enough energy to solve the country's persistent and manifold problems.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Russia's constitutional number two, continued leave near Moscow and some commentators saw it as a sign that it was "business as ususal" at the top.
Financial markets also shrugged off reports on his health, sending Russian markets into record territory on Friday. Some analysts said they expected more enthusiastic buying on Monday.

But neither Chernomyrdin, nor Anatoly Chubais, the powerful head of the Kremlin administration, have commented on Yeltsin's latest illness and NTV said: "Officials do not know what to say. It looks like they are at a loss or even frightened."
The president's latest bout of illness has also opened up a debate on whether Russia should alter its constitution to shift some power from the president to the legislature.
At least one Moscow daily newspaper suggested on Saturday that, because of his prolonged illnesses, it might be time for Yeltsin, post-Soviet Russia's first president, to step down.
"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of state properly," the liberal daily Komsomolskaya Pravda said.

But the mass-circulation Moskovsky Komsomolets said on Sunday the government was working effectively without Yeltsin's participation. "For the last half year, both the country and bureaucrats have got used to the participation in name only of the head of state in the country's affairs," it wrote in a front-page story. "The mechanism of taking decisions has been well-tuned since the time of his absence from the Kremlin."
